units.title: Schematic Basics
units.tip: A schematic is a diagram showing how electronic components connect to each other. Each component has a symbol, and lines show the electrical connections. Schematics are the blueprint for how a circuit works before any physical board is built.

exercises.question: What is a schematic?
exercises.answer: A diagram showing electrical components and how they are connected
exercises.explain: A schematic uses standardized symbols to represent components like resistors, capacitors, and chips. Lines between symbols show electrical connections.
choices: A physical circuit board
A diagram showing electrical components and how they are connected
A list of parts to buy
A mechanical drawing

exercises.question: Why do schematics use standardized symbols?
exercises.answer: So anyone can understand the circuit regardless of their native language
exercises.explain: Standardized symbols are universal. An engineer in any country recognizes a resistor symbol the same way. This makes communication reliable.
choices: To reduce the file size
So anyone can understand the circuit regardless of their native language
Because they are easier to draw by hand
To make the schematic more artistic

exercises.question: What does a 'net' mean in PCB design?
exercises.answer: An electrical connection that groups all points at the same voltage
exercises.explain: A net is a named signal or connection. All wires in a net are electrically equivalent and at the same potential. Nets make it easy to route complex circuits.
choices: A type of via
An electrical connection that groups all points at the same voltage
A fishing tool
A printed circuit board

exercises.question: What is the difference between a schematic and a layout?
exercises.answer: Schematic shows connections; layout shows physical placement on the board
exercises.explain: The schematic defines what connects to what electrically. The layout decides where components go physically on the board and how traces route between them.
choices: Schematic shows connections; layout shows physical placement on the board
Schematics are for professionals; layouts are for beginners
They are the same thing
Layouts are always digital; schematics can be hand-drawn

exercises.question: What is the purpose of ground in a circuit?
exercises.answer: A reference point against which all other voltages are measured
exercises.explain: Ground (GND) is the common return path for current and the baseline (0V) for voltage measurements. All other voltages are measured relative to ground.
choices: To reduce heat in the board
A reference point against which all other voltages are measured
To provide protection in case of electrical shock
To prevent static electricity

exercises.question: Before laying out a board, what must you do first?
exercises.answer: Design and verify the schematic
exercises.explain: The schematic is the logical blueprint. If the schematic is wrong, the board will be wrong. Always verify the circuit works on paper before committing it to a board.
choices: Apply for a patent
Choose the board size
Design and verify the schematic
Buy all the parts

exercises.question: What is a 'reference designator' in a schematic?
exercises.answer: The label that identifies each component, like R1, C2, U3
exercises.explain: Reference designators are unique labels for every component. R means resistor, C means capacitor, U means integrated circuit. The number makes each one unique.
choices: The price of the component
The country where the component is made
The label that identifies each component, like R1, C2, U3
A document that comes with the component

exercises.question: What is a 'datasheet'?
exercises.answer: Technical documentation describing a component's pins, ratings, and behavior
exercises.explain: A datasheet is the official specification for a component. It shows pin definitions, voltage/current limits, and how to use it correctly.
choices: Technical documentation describing a component's pins, ratings, and behavior
A schematic symbol
A list of components to order
A design template

exercises.question: Why should you check datasheets before designing?
exercises.answer: To understand pin assignments, voltage limits, and electrical requirements
exercises.explain: The datasheet tells you what each pin does, the maximum voltage/current it can handle, and any special requirements. Skipping this step causes designs to fail.
choices: Because the internet says you should
To impress your boss
To understand pin assignments, voltage limits, and electrical requirements
Because datasheets are free to download

exercises.question: What does 'schematic capture' mean?
exercises.answer: Using software to draw the circuit schematic
exercises.explain: Schematic capture is the process of using PCB design software to draw your circuit schematically. The software tracks components, nets, and generates a parts list.
choices: Using software to draw the circuit schematic
Taking a photo of a circuit board
Building a prototype by hand
Copying someone else's design

units.title: Components and Footprints
units.tip: Components are the physical parts (resistors, chips, connectors) that go on a board. Each component has a footprint, which is the pattern of solder pads that matches the component's physical shape. The footprint must match the component exactly.

exercises.question: What is a 'package' in PCB design?
exercises.answer: The physical form of a component and its pin arrangement
exercises.explain: A package defines the physical shape and pin layout of a component. The same chip might come in DIP-8, TQFP-32, or other packages depending on the application.
choices: A collection of design rules
The physical form of a component and its pin arrangement
The datasheet
The shipping box the component arrives in

exercises.question: What does DIP stand for?
exercises.answer: Dual In-Line Package, with two rows of pins
exercises.explain: DIP packages have pins on opposite sides in two parallel rows. DIP-8 has 8 pins total (4 on each side). They are easy to insert into breadboards.
choices: Double Internal Pin
Double Input Package
Digital Interface Protocol
Dual In-Line Package, with two rows of pins

exercises.question: What is a 'footprint'?
exercises.answer: The pattern of solder pads on a PCB that matches a component's physical shape
exercises.explain: A footprint is the outline and pad pattern for one component. It defines where solder pads go and their spacing so the component fits correctly.
choices: The pattern of solder pads on a PCB that matches a component's physical shape
The manufacturing date
The weight of a component
The size of the component's packaging box

exercises.question: Why is it critical that a footprint matches the component exactly?
exercises.answer: A wrong footprint prevents the component from soldering properly or fitting at all
exercises.explain: If the footprint pads are too far apart or too close, the component will not fit or will not solder. A mismatch means a non-working board.
choices: A wrong footprint prevents the component from soldering properly or fitting at all
Because footprints determine the component's cost
To fill up PCB design software
Because footprints affect the circuit's speed

exercises.question: What is the difference between through-hole and surface-mount packages?
exercises.answer: Through-hole uses pins through the board; surface-mount sits on top
exercises.explain: Through-hole components have long pins that go through the board. Surface-mount components sit flat on the board surface. Surface-mount is smaller and faster to assemble.
choices: They require different soldering temperatures
Through-hole is newer technology
Surface-mount is more expensive
Through-hole uses pins through the board; surface-mount sits on top

exercises.question: What does 'component placement' mean?
exercises.answer: Deciding where each component goes on the PCB layout
exercises.explain: Component placement is the first step of board layout. You position each component to minimize trace length, avoid noise, and create a logical flow.
choices: Deciding where each component goes on the PCB layout
Ordering components from suppliers
Testing the component before use
Writing the schematic symbol

exercises.question: Why should you group related components together?
exercises.answer: To minimize trace length and reduce noise and interference
exercises.explain: Grouping related components close together keeps signal paths short, reduces capacitive coupling, and makes the board more compact and reliable.
choices: To minimize trace length and reduce noise and interference
Because the PCB software requires it
Because it looks more organized
To reduce the board cost

exercises.question: What is a 'critical signal path'?
exercises.answer: A high-speed or sensitive signal that must be routed carefully
exercises.explain: Critical paths (like clock signals or analog signals) need short, direct traces to avoid noise. These get priority during board layout.
choices: Any signal on the board
A signal that repeats in the schematic
A high-speed or sensitive signal that must be routed carefully
A signal that crosses the entire board

exercises.question: What does 'DFM' (Design For Manufacturing) mean?
exercises.answer: Designing the board so it is easy and cost-effective to manufacture
exercises.explain: DFM considers manufacturing constraints: minimum trace width, minimum pad size, assembly capabilities. Good DFM reduces waste and cost.
choices: Designing the board so it is easy and cost-effective to manufacture
Double Failure Mode
Data File Management
Digital Frequency Modulation

exercises.question: When placing components, what should you avoid?
exercises.answer: Placing high-noise components near sensitive analog circuits
exercises.explain: Digital circuits (especially clocks and high-speed logic) generate noise. Placing them far from sensitive analog circuits prevents interference.
choices: Placing high-noise components near sensitive analog circuits
Placing anything on the left side of the board
Placing too many components in one area
Placing expensive components first

units.title: Traces and Routing
units.tip: Traces are the thin copper lines that connect components on a PCB. Routing is the process of drawing these connections. Good routing minimizes length, avoids crossing signals, and respects electrical rules.

exercises.question: What is a 'trace'?
exercises.answer: A copper conductor on a PCB that carries current between pads
exercises.explain: Traces are thin copper paths etched onto the board. They replace wires and carry signals and power between component pads.
choices: A design rule
A debugging tool
A type of solder
A copper conductor on a PCB that carries current between pads

exercises.question: What does 'trace width' affect?
exercises.answer: How much current the trace can safely carry without overheating
exercises.explain: Thicker traces carry more current before exceeding safe temperatures. The required width depends on the current and copper thickness.
choices: The color of the PCB
How much current the trace can safely carry without overheating
The speed of signals on the trace
The manufacturing time

exercises.question: What is 'trace length matching'?
exercises.answer: Making multiple traces the same length to match signal arrival times
exercises.explain: High-speed buses (like DDR memory) require equal-length traces so all data bits arrive at the same time. Mismatched lengths cause timing skew.
choices: Selecting trace color to be consistent
Making multiple traces the same length to match signal arrival times
Organizing traces in parallel rows
Making all traces on a board the same length

exercises.question: What is 'trace impedance'?
exercises.answer: The resistance and reactance of a trace at high frequencies
exercises.explain: At high speeds, traces act like transmission lines with impedance. Matching impedance to the driver and receiver prevents reflections that corrupt signals.
choices: The color of the solder mask
The resistance and reactance of a trace at high frequencies
The ability of a trace to carry DC current
The physical width of the trace

exercises.question: When do you need to be most careful about two signal traces crossing over each other on different layers?
exercises.answer: When the signals are sensitive or run at very high speeds
exercises.explain: Traces on the same layer cannot cross without shorting, so crossings happen on different layers. Overlapping sensitive or very fast signals can couple and cause crosstalk. Cross them at right angles or separate them with a plane.
choices: Never, it is never a problem
When the signals are sensitive or run at very high speeds
Always, no exceptions
Only on the top layer

exercises.question: What is 'auto-routing' in PCB design?
exercises.answer: Software that automatically finds paths for traces between pads
exercises.explain: Auto-routers use algorithms to find valid trace paths. They are fast but often suboptimal. Manual routing gives better results for complex boards.
choices: Software that automatically finds paths for traces between pads
A layout template for standard circuits
A type of soldering tool
Drawing all traces by hand

exercises.question: What is a 'rat's nest'?
exercises.answer: The unrouted connections shown as lines between component pads
exercises.explain: Before routing, PCB software shows all required connections as straight lines. As you route traces, the rat's nest shrinks until all nets are connected.
choices: An obsolete PCB format
The unrouted connections shown as lines between component pads
A design error
Tangled traces that do not work

exercises.question: What does '45-degree routing' mean?
exercises.answer: Routing traces at 45-degree angles instead of 90 degrees where possible
exercises.explain: Sharp 90-degree corners are avoided because they can trap etchant during manufacturing and make the trace slightly less uniform. 45-degree bends are the usual preference, and they also keep traces a bit shorter.
choices: Making all angles exactly 45 degrees
A rule for spacing traces apart
Routing traces at 45-degree angles instead of 90 degrees where possible
A type of solder joint

exercises.question: What is 'fan-out' in PCB layout?
exercises.answer: Spreading out traces from a dense component or pad to minimize congestion
exercises.explain: High pin-count chips have many pads close together. Fan-out spreads these connections apart so they can route to other parts of the board without crossing.
choices: The angle of a trace bend
A routing error
The number of traces connected to a pad
Spreading out traces from a dense component or pad to minimize congestion

exercises.question: What should you do if two traces must cross?
exercises.answer: Route them on different layers using vias to separate them
exercises.explain: If two nets must cross, put one on a different layer. Vias connect the layers. This avoids electrical shorts between the crossing traces.
choices: Accept the short and shield it
Route them on different layers using vias to separate them
Redesign the board to avoid it
Use a thinner trace

units.title: Layers and Ground Planes
units.tip: PCBs can have multiple copper layers stacked together. Ground planes are large sheets of copper connected to ground that act as a reference and return path. They reduce noise and improve signal integrity.

exercises.question: What is a multi-layer PCB?
exercises.answer: A board with multiple copper layers stacked and separated by insulation
exercises.explain: A 4-layer board has 4 copper layers (typically top, ground, power, bottom). More layers allow denser routing and better signal integrity.
choices: A board with many components
A board with multiple solder masks
A board with multiple copper layers stacked and separated by insulation
A board made of multiple materials

exercises.question: What are the typical layers in a 4-layer board?
exercises.answer: Top signal, ground plane, power plane, bottom signal
exercises.explain: This arrangement sandwiches power and ground planes between signal layers. This provides a low-impedance path for current return.
choices: 4 signal layers
Ground, ground, signal, signal
Power, signal, signal, power
Top signal, ground plane, power plane, bottom signal

exercises.question: What is a 'ground plane'?
exercises.answer: A large sheet of copper connected to ground that serves as a reference and return path
exercises.explain: A ground plane is a continuous copper layer (or large area) connected to ground. It provides a low-impedance return path for signals and reduces noise.
choices: A type of solder
A flat area with no components
A large sheet of copper connected to ground that serves as a reference and return path
A layer that must be removed

exercises.question: What is a 'via'?
exercises.answer: A small hole drilled through a PCB connecting copper on different layers
exercises.explain: Vias allow signals and power to move between layers. A via is a connection point from one layer to another.
choices: A type of trace
A design rule
A small hole drilled through a PCB connecting copper on different layers
An error in the layout

exercises.question: Why should power and ground planes be continuous and unbroken?
exercises.answer: To minimize impedance and provide low-resistance current paths
exercises.explain: Cuts and islands in power or ground planes increase impedance and create loops that radiate noise. Continuous planes give the return current a short, low-impedance path.
choices: To reduce the board cost
Because the software requires it
To minimize impedance and provide low-resistance current paths
To save time during design

exercises.question: What is a 'decoupling capacitor'?
exercises.answer: A capacitor placed near a chip's power pins to filter noise and supply current spikes
exercises.explain: Decoupling caps absorb sudden current surges from logic transitions. They smooth the power supply and reduce voltage spikes that cause errors.
choices: A capacitor placed near a chip's power pins to filter noise and supply current spikes
A device that measures capacitance
A capacitor that blocks power from the chip
A type of resistor

exercises.question: How many decoupling capacitors do you typically need per chip?
exercises.answer: At least one, often multiple values to cover different frequencies
exercises.explain: A single capacitor per power pin is a minimum. Using multiple capacitor values (100nF, 10uF) covers a wider frequency range and works better.
choices: Exactly one per chip
Decoupling caps are optional
At least one, often multiple values to cover different frequencies
The number depends on the trace width

exercises.question: Where should decoupling capacitors be placed?
exercises.answer: As close as possible to the chip's power pins
exercises.explain: Close placement minimizes lead inductance and keeps the capacitor effective at high frequencies. Distance reduces the capacitor's benefit.
choices: Under the solder mask
Far from the chip to reduce heat
As close as possible to the chip's power pins
Anywhere on the board

exercises.question: What is 'star grounding'?
exercises.answer: Connecting all ground paths to a single point to avoid ground loops
exercises.explain: In single-layer or simple boards, star grounding prevents loops that cause noise. All ground returns meet at one point, then go to the power supply.
choices: Grounding all components at once
Connecting all ground paths to a single point to avoid ground loops
Grounding only high-power components
Using star-shaped circuit symbols

exercises.question: What is 'power distribution network' (PDN) impedance?
exercises.answer: The total impedance from the power supply to a component, affecting voltage stability
exercises.explain: PDN impedance determines how well the power system responds to current spikes. Lower impedance means better voltage stability and fewer errors.
choices: The total impedance from the power supply to a component, affecting voltage stability
The resistance of power traces only
A type of capacitor rating
The efficiency of the power supply

units.title: Design for Manufacturing
units.tip: Design for Manufacturing (DFM) considers how a board is physically made and assembled. Understanding soldering, component mounting, and assembly processes ensures your design can be built correctly and cost-effectively.

exercises.question: What is the advantage of through-hole assembly?
exercises.answer: Strong mechanical connections and easy hand-soldering
exercises.explain: Through-hole pins go through the board and bend on the back, creating strong mechanical joints. They tolerate larger thermal stresses than surface-mount.
choices: It requires less copper
It is faster to manufacture
Strong mechanical connections and easy hand-soldering
It uses less power

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of surface-mount assembly?
exercises.answer: Small size, fast automated assembly, and high component density
exercises.explain: Surface-mount components are tiny and placed by pick-and-place robots. This allows higher density, faster production, and smaller boards.
choices: Lower cost components
Small size, fast automated assembly, and high component density
Easier to repair by hand
Stronger mechanical joints

exercises.question: What is 'reflow soldering'?
exercises.answer: Heating the entire board in an oven to melt solder and attach surface-mount parts
exercises.explain: Reflow soldering heats the board to above solder's melting point, then cools it. All surface-mount components solder simultaneously in one pass.
choices: Applying solder to wires instead of pads
Soldering by hand with an iron
Heating the entire board in an oven to melt solder and attach surface-mount parts
Using a wave of liquid solder to coat the board

exercises.question: What is 'wave soldering'?
exercises.answer: Passing the board over a wave of molten solder to solder through-hole components
exercises.explain: Wave soldering is used for through-hole assembly. The board moves over a wave of hot solder, which wets the pads and solders all pins at once.
choices: Using ultrasonic vibration to solder parts
Hand-soldering each joint
Soldering surface-mount components
Passing the board over a wave of molten solder to solder through-hole components

exercises.question: What is a 'solder pad'?
exercises.answer: A small copper area on the PCB where a component lead attaches and is soldered
exercises.explain: Solder pads are tiny copper areas with specific sizes and shapes. Solder flows onto these pads, creating the electrical and mechanical bond with component leads.
choices: A small copper area on the PCB where a component lead attaches and is soldered
An insulating layer
A place to store solder
A type of circuit board

exercises.question: How do you find the minimum trace width you can use on a board?
exercises.answer: Check the capabilities published by your chosen manufacturer
exercises.explain: Manufacturing capabilities vary from one fabricator and process to another. Check the manufacturer's specifications before setting your design rules. Finer traces usually cost more; coarser traces are cheaper and more forgiving.
choices: There is no minimum
It is the same for every manufacturer
It is set by the schematic symbol
Check the capabilities published by your chosen manufacturer

exercises.question: What is 'design rule check' (DRC)?
exercises.answer: Automated verification that traces, pads, and spacing meet manufacturing requirements
exercises.explain: DRC software checks that traces are not too thin, spacing is not too tight, and all pads are properly sized. It prevents designs that cannot be fabricated.
choices: Automated verification that traces, pads, and spacing meet manufacturing requirements
A debugging tool
A list of electrical rules
A manual inspection process

exercises.question: What does 'clearance' mean in PCB design?
exercises.answer: The minimum distance between copper elements to prevent shorts
exercises.explain: Clearance is the gap between traces, between a trace and a pad, or between a pad and the board edge. Insufficient clearance causes electrical shorts.
choices: The distance from the board edge
The amount of empty space on a board
The space inside a via
The minimum distance between copper elements to prevent shorts

exercises.question: What is a 'solder mask'?
exercises.answer: A layer of insulation that covers copper except where solder joints go
exercises.explain: Solder mask prevents solder bridges between nearby traces and protects copper from oxidation. It is typically green, but other colors are available.
choices: A protective tool used during assembly
A type of component
A photographic negative
A layer of insulation that covers copper except where solder joints go

exercises.question: What is the purpose of 'silk screen' (legend layer) on a PCB?
exercises.answer: To print component labels, reference designators, and test points
exercises.explain: Silk screen is white printing on the PCB surface. It shows component labels (R1, C2), logos, and test points to aid assembly and troubleshooting.
choices: To insulate the board
To improve electrical performance
To hold components in place during soldering
To print component labels, reference designators, and test points

units.title: Verification and Quality
units.tip: Before manufacturing, a PCB design must be checked for errors and verified to work. Design reviews, simulations, and final checks catch problems early.

exercises.question: What is a 'design review'?
exercises.answer: A systematic examination of the schematic and layout for errors
exercises.explain: A design review involves checking logic, component choices, routing, and manufacturing rules. Having a second set of eyes catches mistakes.
choices: Testing the finished board
Ordering parts from suppliers
Painting the board
A systematic examination of the schematic and layout for errors

exercises.question: What is 'electrical rule check' (ERC)?
exercises.answer: Automated verification of schematic connections for electrical errors
exercises.explain: ERC checks for unconnected pins, duplicate net names, shorted power/ground, and other wiring errors in the schematic.
choices: A type of cable
A way to estimate manufacturing cost
Testing the board under power
Automated verification of schematic connections for electrical errors

exercises.question: What is a 'prototype' in PCB design?
exercises.answer: A small run of boards built for testing before full manufacturing
exercises.explain: A prototype is a test board to verify the design works. If problems are found, they are fixed in software and a corrected production run is made.
choices: A computer simulation
A schematic diagram
A small run of boards built for testing before full manufacturing
The original hand-drawn design

exercises.question: What is 'simulation' in circuit design?
exercises.answer: Using software to model circuit behavior without building it
exercises.explain: SPICE simulators predict how a circuit will behave: voltages, currents, timing. This catches errors before the prototype is built.
choices: Running the design in an oven
Using software to model circuit behavior without building it
Building multiple versions
Testing on a breadboard

exercises.question: What does 'net list' verify?
exercises.answer: That the layout matches the schematic connections
exercises.explain: The net list is a record of all connections from the schematic. It is compared with the layout to ensure nothing was misrouted.
choices: That all components are available
That the traces are not too thin
That the layout matches the schematic connections
That the board can support high current

exercises.question: What is 'continuity testing'?
exercises.answer: Verifying that electrical paths exist where they should and shorts do not
exercises.explain: Continuity testing uses a multimeter to check that traces are connected and no accidental shorts exist between signals.
choices: Testing whether the board is still in production
Counting the number of components
Measuring trace thickness
Verifying that electrical paths exist where they should and shorts do not

exercises.question: What is 'in-circuit testing' (ICT)?
exercises.answer: Automated testing of a board with a fixture that checks every node
exercises.explain: ICT uses spring-loaded probes (the fixture) to contact test pads on the board. A tester checks voltages, continuity, and component values.
choices: Testing only the circuit diagram
Automated testing of a board with a fixture that checks every node
Testing with the board powered off
A type of solder inspection

exercises.question: What is a 'test point'?
exercises.answer: A pad added to the board for test probes to measure voltage or current
exercises.explain: Test points are marked on silk screen and connected to key signals. They let technicians measure the board during assembly and troubleshooting.
choices: A color marking on the PCB
The highest score on a test
A corner of the board
A pad added to the board for test probes to measure voltage or current

exercises.question: What does 'burn-in' testing do?
exercises.answer: Runs boards at elevated temperature and stress to find early failures
exercises.explain: Burn-in stresses components by running them hot. Weak components fail early in the lab, not in the field.
choices: Runs boards at elevated temperature and stress to find early failures
Measures component temperatures
Removes solder paste residue
Destroys defective boards

exercises.question: What is 'visual inspection' (VI) of a PCB?
exercises.answer: Examining the board with eyes or a microscope for assembly defects
exercises.explain: Visual inspection checks for cold solder joints, bridges, component placement errors, and damaged traces. It can catch many problems before testing.
choices: Examining the board with eyes or a microscope for assembly defects
Testing with power applied
Checking the color of the board
Measuring electrical performance
